tagline: The world’s largest metropolis blends neon futurism with deep tradition — and record numbers of visitors are arriving to see it. It is ranked #10 on Time Out's Best Cities 2026 list.
overview: Despite earthquakes, tsunamis and typhoons, Tokyo has long held on to its top spot as one of the safest metropolises on the planet — young kids still ride the subway to school alone, a small daily miracle for visitors from almost anywhere else. And since Japan reopened its borders, the world has come flooding back: a record roughly 37 million visitors arrived in 2024, drawn by a weak yen and a city that keeps topping itself.

The boom has fueled a construction wave across the skyline. Azabudai Hills opened with the relocated teamLab Borderless digital art museum inside, redeveloped Shibuya keeps adding rooftop observatories above its famous scramble crossing, and Ginza Six anchors a shopping scene that still ranks among the world’s best.

Underneath the neon, the classics hold their ground: the forested calm of the Meiji Shrine, Senso-ji’s incense-filled approach in Asakusa, and roughly 100,000 restaurants — more Michelin stars than Paris — spanning ramen counters to omakase you’ll need to book weeks ahead.

Getting around is half the experience: Haneda keeps the city connected, the Yamanote Line loops every major district, and day trips to Nikko, Hakone or Kamakura put mountains, hot springs and temples within an easy hour of Shinjuku.

funFacts.title: Tokyo means "eastern capital"
funFacts.text: The name Tokyo means "eastern capital". The city, then called Edo, was already one of the world's largest by the 18th century, and Greater Tokyo is now the most populous metropolitan area on Earth.

funFacts.title: Tokyo used to be called Edo
funFacts.text: Edo grew from a small fishing village into the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns, who ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867 while the emperor stayed in Kyoto. After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, the emperor moved to Edo and the city was renamed Tokyo.

funFacts.title: Hotels staffed by robots
funFacts.text: The Henn na Hotel chain, which has a branch in Ginza, uses robot receptionists that check guests in. The first Henn na Hotel opened near Nagasaki in 2015 and was recognised by Guinness as the first hotel staffed by robots.

funFacts.title: Calming blue lights
funFacts.text: Some Tokyo train platforms have blue lights at the ends, installed because studies suggested blue light can have a calming effect and help reduce suicide attempts.

funFacts.title: Vending machines everywhere
funFacts.text: Japan has millions of vending machines, and Tokyo seems to have one on every corner. Besides drinks, they can sell hot meals, umbrellas, ice cream and even fresh fruit.

funFacts.title: The world's Michelin star capital
funFacts.text: Tokyo has more Michelin-starred restaurants than any other city in the world, with around 200 starred restaurants in recent editions of the guide.

funFacts.title: Tokyo Tower beats the Eiffel Tower
funFacts.text: Tokyo Tower, finished in 1958, was inspired by the Eiffel Tower and is slightly taller at 333 metres. It is painted orange and white to meet air-safety rules. Tokyo Skytree, at 634 metres, is now the tallest tower in the world.

funFacts.title: The world's largest metropolis
funFacts.text: With more than 37 million people, Greater Tokyo is the most populous urban area in the world. Despite the crowds, the city is famously clean, orderly and efficient.

funFacts.title: One of the world's safest cities
funFacts.text: Tokyo regularly ranks among the safest big cities in the world. It is common to see people napping on trains or leaving bags to save a café seat.

funFacts.title: Tax-free shopping for visitors
funFacts.text: Visitors to Japan can shop tax-free at participating stores on purchases of 5,000 yen or more. Bring your passport, which is required for tax-free purchases.

Tokyo has vending machines everywhere - one for every 23 people in the city.
The Imperial Palace in Tokyo sits on the site of the former Edo Castle.
Tokyo's Akihabara district is the center of anime, manga, and electronics culture.
Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964 and again in 2021.
The cherry blossom season in Tokyo attracts millions of visitors each spring.
Tokyo has more neon signs than any other city in the world.

Tokyo's train system is so punctual that average delays are less than 20 seconds.
Harajuku district in Tokyo is famous for its unique street fashion and youth culture.
